destination.title: Police Skipped His Rights — Then He Learned He Couldn't Even Sue

short46: An officer questions you.
He never reads you your rights.
Your own written words go on trial.
Can you make him pay for that?
In Los Angeles a hospital worker was
questioned by a sheriff's deputy.
No warning no right to stay silent
was ever spoken.
He wrote a statement and it was
used against him at trial.
A jury heard everything and set him free.
So he sued the deputy for money
under a civil rights law for the
warning that never came.
Twice juries sided with the officer.
An appeals court said that missing warning
could support the lawsuit.
So the deputy asked the Supreme Court
to step in.
In 2022 the Court ruled six to three.
Skipping the Miranda warning by itself is
not something you can sue an officer over.
But Miranda still stands.
Your unwarned words can still be kept
out of your trial.
A right is not the same as a payout.
Watch the full case on the channel.
Follow for more.

candidate_payload_lines: Central question (cold open then payoff): If an officer never reads you your rights, can you make that officer answer for it, by himself, in a civil suit for money?
Answer delivered in ending: For the failure to warn, standing alone, you cannot sue the officer for civil money damages under Section 1983.
And the warning you can recite from memory, the one you have heard in a thousand arrests on a thousand screens, never came.
If they never read you your rights, and your own words go on trial in your place, can you ever make them answer for that?
Almost no one has ever been shown where the protection stops.
It runs from a signature on a hospital table all the way to the highest court in the country, and it ends on a line almost no one has ever had drawn for them.
In 2014, inside a medical center in Los Angeles, a man named Terence Tekoh went to work.
Before a single question was asked, no one told Terence Tekoh that he could stay silent.
No one told him the page he was filling out could one day be carried into a courtroom and read aloud to the people deciding whether he walked free.
Section 1983 was written in the raw years after the Civil War to give ordinary people a way into federal court when the state itself becomes the wrongdoer.
It ruled that using such a statement against a defendant at trial could violate the Fifth Amendment, and could support a lawsuit under Section 1983.
Nobody in that courtroom was fighting about the famous case.
In 1966, in Miranda versus Arizona, the Supreme Court held that before police question someone who is in custody, they have to deliver the warnings you already know.
No one was fighting about a second, quieter decision either.
In the year 2000, in a ruling called Dickerson, the Court confirmed that Miranda was not a suggestion or a courtesy.
And Section 1983 exists precisely so a person can sue for the loss of a constitutional right.
Picture a protective fence built around a deeper right, the Fifth Amendment promise that no one can force you to incriminate yourself.
And an injury that is not a constitutional violation is not the kind of harm Section 1983 was ever built to repair.

shorts.angle: Justice Alito's majority called the Miranda warnings a protective fence around the Fifth Amendment, and everything else followed from that one distinction.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short states the outcome, that a skipped warning is not something you can sue over; this cut is the single legal move the majority used to get there.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If the warning is only a fence, what happens to the earlier ruling that called Miranda a constitutional rule?

lines.text: The Supreme Court took away the right to sue over a skipped Miranda warning using one metaphor.
source_lines: Writing for six of the nine justices, Justice Samuel Alito drew a distinction that is careful, technical, and enormous for you.

lines.text: Writing for six justices, Justice Samuel Alito called the warnings prophylactic rules. Picture a protective fence built around a deeper right.
source_lines: Miranda's warnings, he wrote, are what lawyers call prophylactic rules. Picture a protective fence built around a deeper right, the Fifth Amendment promise that no one can force you to incriminate yourself.

lines.text: The Fifth Amendment promise that no one can force you to incriminate yourself. The warnings guard that inner right. But they are not the right. A fence, not the ground it stands on.
source_lines: The warnings guard that inner right. But the warnings themselves, the majority reasoned, are not the constitutional right. A fence. Not the ground it stands on.

lines.text: From that one distinction the rest follows. Failing to give the warnings is not, on its own, a violation of the Constitution. So there is nothing to pay for.
source_lines: From that one distinction, the rest follows.
then failing to give them is not, on its own, a violation of the Constitution
So the deputy could not be made to pay money damages simply because the warning had been left out.

lines.text: Three justices refused to accept that. A right nobody can enforce, they warned in dissent, slowly stops feeling like a right at all.
source_lines: Three justices refused to accept that.

Take away the ability to sue, and some people whose rights are genuinely broken will be left standing there with nothing to collect, and no one to answer for it.
